Speech:
The thrust of my remarks is not to say that we are happy. If the hon. member listens to my entire speech, I think he will get the thrust of my remarks. In fact, very shortly I will refer to an article which will provide the thrust of my remarks. Basically, it is that the doom and gloom which comes from the other side really does not make much sense. Nobody likes a gross national debt of $80 billion, but the point of the matter is that $80 billion represents 26 per cent or 27 per cent of the gross national product, and if we go back to 1962, it was about 30 per cent of the gross national product. It is the relative thing about which I am talking. That is what is left out of a lot of the neo-conservative comments, which I will illustrate in a minute.
I should like to look at the purchases of Petro-Canada. I hear people talk about some large oil company, such as Mobil or Gulf, buying and investing in the holdings of some other company; it may very well be the Thomson chain investing in Hudson's Bay. This is an investment. Thomson did not go out and spend $400 million or whatever; he invested it. When we went out and bought Atlantic Richfield in 1976, I believe we paid $340 million. I am told it is now worth about $1 billion. Is that a good investment? Certainly there must be a reason for it being worth a good deal more. Of course, I think one of the reasons is that all corporations in the oil industry are worth a great deal more. But in late 1978 or early 1979 I remember Morty Shulman saying to me on his show, "You threw away a lot of money; it was a waste of money", and today we are told that it is worth 2.5 times what it was then. If that is the case, how can one call it a bad investment? I would say that the people who sold it might very well have been skinned at that rate; if a company can appreciate 250 per cent in the course of two or three years.
It seems when the federal government purchases a company it is spending money. No one ever talks about the investment or what will be the return to Canadian people. They do not talk about those things. It is all right for the Alberta government to buy PWA; it seems fair enough. But when the federal government does it it is some kind of crime. Those mathematics always bother me.
Over the weekend when I was preparing for this particular speech, I noticed an article which appeared in The Globe and

February 16, 1981
Borrowing Authority
Mail. In fact I was surprised to find it in The Globe. I always suspect that Rupert Murdoch has secretly bought The Globe and it is now a new paper. At any rate, I should like to refer to the article by Lawrence Martin in Washington. He said:
Ronald Reagan tells the country it is in its worst economic mess since the Great Depression. He lofts a 1960 dollar on the television screen and, illustrating the nation's misery, demonstrates that it is only worth 36 cents today. He says that big government is at the root of most of the country's economic problems. He vows to take a meat axe to the budget.
Let us take a look at that in terms of American funds at this particular point in time.
In 1960 when a dollar was worth a dollar, the median family income in the United States was roughly $5,000 a year. In 1979, the median income was $19,000 a year. Nineteen thousand dollars worth 36 cents each comes out to $6,840 real 1960 dollars. In those terms, the standard of living, despite what the president tells the people, has risen sharply-by almost a third.
So, the American people are better off by a third. In 1960, in terms of 1971 fixed dollars, our gross national product was $53 billion. In 1975, in terms of 1971 fixed dollars, our gross national product was $110 billion. In that period of time we see a doubling. We can certainly say that Canadians are far better off than we were in 1960, in spite of the kind of thinking put forward by the Conservatives.
Mr. Martin in his article says:
Myth No. 2 that the new administration is trying to pass off is that big government and its deficits are the prime cause of inflation. The new-right Reaganites have such deep faith in this theory that it is the one prong of their one-pronged anti-inflation program.
Basically, that is what I have heard from the opposite side of the House since 1974-75. Mr. Martin in his article goes on to ask about oil prices and food prices.
At this point let us take Vancouver as an example. What about the land which is being bought by people from Hong Kong, and Alberta, which is pushing prices up tremendously? There you have a situation of tremendous tension brought on by super-inflation. It is not caused by government. These are real inflationary effects which are structural in nature. They can be defined very easily. The increase in oil by seven or eight times has a tremendous effect on inflation. To say that there is really only one inflationary factor does not make sense.
Mr. Martin's article goes on:
Myth No. 3 is that government has grown so big that it is out of control. In fact, government hasn't grown so much.

We will proceed with significant support from the provinces. I believe, and the hon. member for Provencher has confirmed this in his remarks, that we are proceeding with a charter of rights which has the support of the people of
Canada.
Of course, there are people who are unhappy with the process by which we have arrived at this position. I am unhappy with it. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) is unhappy with it. We would all prefer to go with the support of all the provinces. We would have loved to do that. The reason we are proceeding in the way we are is that we recognize that that kind of support is impossible to achieve.
Nor is this new Constitution one which is being made, as was charged yesterday, by foreigners, by the Imperial Parliament, by Great Britain. This Constitution is being made in Canada. Indeed, it has the longest gestation period of any baby in public life, going back well over 50 years. It is being made by the members of this House of Commons in this debate and by the decisions they will take. It has been made by the past Members of Parliament in previous parliamentary discussions, by the work of at least two joint committees of Parliament which have assessed our Constitution, by the continuing participation of a whole host of interested groups who made their views known to the joint committee, and by the witnesses who appeared before it. The role of Great Britain in this process is a formal one, not the exercise of moral authority. It is rather like a notary who ratifies a contract or a civil authority which registers a marriage.
There has been much talk, I think wildly exaggerated, on the part of the opposition about the divisiveness of this process that we have gone through, about the strength of debate and discussion taking place in the country. That is not a source of divisiveness. It is not a source of weakness. It is a source of strength that in this country we freely, forcefully, frankly and passionately debate these views. I suspect there is no institution which expresses more strongly a conflict of views of
The Constitution
various representatives than this House of Parliament, this House of Commons. The expression of those views in this manner is not divisiveness. It is a way in which we come to a conclusion and develop consensus for our policies.
It is now before the House of Commons. It is not the process, not the manner of arriving, but the substance. What we must decide is whether in our heart of hearts the substance of what is being proposed is what we want for Canadians and what Canadians want for themselves.
The official spokesman for the Conservatives has said they want entrenched rights, but not by this process, even though he believes an entrenched charter of rights has popular support. This is a serious matter, but perhaps once in a while we can look at serious matters lightly. I could not help but think yesterday that I was rather happy the hon. member for Provencher was not around when Moses came down from Sinai because he would have said: "Of course, we are all in favour of the Ten Commandments, but we think Moses went up the wrong mountain, took the wrong path or should have had someone with him and, in any case, all of the tribes should be able to opt out." That is a lighthearted view. I see by his smile that the hon. member appreciates that, but the point 1 want to make is that it is the substance on which the House must now pronounce. It is the question of whether we want these rights made legally enforceable for Canadians.

I should now like to share with the House what lessons I have learned. This country, Canada, Mr. Speaker, was not built in ease and euphoria. The French settlers who came in the seventeenth century had to fight against a hostile environment at the cost of hardships difficult to imagine today before taking root in this land. In the eighteenth century, confrontation with a new occupant was a constant source of political tensions.
The rebellion of 1837 and the struggles for a responsible government took up the nineteenth century until confederation. Since 1867, Canada has witnessed a slow and lengthy process of political evolution. Step by step, it has won its autonomy, its independence, its sovereignty. Today, we have come to the last stage of the old era and the start of the new. We now face a choice, a fundamental one. We must decide what kind of country we want to build. That choice cannot be easy or devoid of growing pains. No country in the world has ever won its official independence without difficulty, without debate, without emotion, without passion. Those who would imagine that the Fathers of Confederation conceived the federal union of this country in easy discussions, in social gatherings at Charlottetown or at Quebec should read again those pages of our history. Those who would believe that the people took an active part in the efforts that led to the birth of Canada are totally mistaken. In fact, the public was almost completely excluded.
On November 7, 1864, Antoine Aime Dorion, the hon. member for Hochelaga, my predecessor in this House, denounced before his electors the secret nature of the confederation debates saying, and I quote:
You already know that a conference was held in Quebec City ... The highest interests of the country were discussed at meetings held in camera ... Had the Prime Minister and the government stopped with the first page of that tabled document, we would then be following past, well-established and proper practices, because that first page deals only with regional ministers. Therefore, when the constitutional proposals were introduced last fall, it was with particular pleasure that I noted there would be such a charter in this proposal.
It was, however, very discouraging when reading the fine print of the charter to discover how hastily conceived it had been and to what a large extent it had neglected the real needs of many Canadians. Indeed, in my speech in the House of Commons on October 23, I pointed out in particular that the charter, whatever its intent, did not guarantee women's human right to equality. National Energy Board Act
73(1) The provisions of this part that provide negotiation and arbitration procedures to determine compensation matters apply in respect of all damage caused by the pipeline of a company or anything carried by the pipeline but do not apply to
(a)	claims against a company arising out of activities of the company unless those activities are directly related to

The current political and military situation in El Salvador is obviously highly fluid and we are not in a position to make assessments on the basis of first-hand information. However, our policy is not confused. On the contrary, it has been clear, concise and consistent. Throughout this period it has been the Canadian government's policy not to supply arms to either side in El Salvador or to any other country in Central America. I might say that there was a grievous error recently in the Toronto Globe and Mail in which it stated to the contrary. The information was obtained as a result of a reporter reading the wrong column in a series
El Salvador
of statistics, but the newspaper has never bothered to correct the record. The policy has thus been consistently implemented, and press reports to the contrary are quite inaccurate.
We do not believe that the problems of El Salvador can be resolved by military measures. We urge all other governments to follow the same policy and refrain from supplying offensive weapons, the use of which only causes increased violence and suffering for the people of El Salvador. We strongly support the traditional principle of international law, which is one of opposition to any interference from the outside in another country's domestic affairs.
We also believe that the problems of El Salvador can be solved only through political discussion and negotiation by the Salvadorian parties directly concerned. 1 explained this to the representatives of the revolutionary forces when 1 met with them in January. I also explained it to Secretary Haig in Washington. I have explained it to the House, and I have explained it many times to the Canadian news media. It will serve no useful purpose to engage in public denunciations. 1 can assure the House that we will continue to make our views in this regard known in bilateral contacts with the United States and in the appropriate multilateral fora, as we have done in the past, as and when appropriate.
We fully share the sentiments of hon. members with respect to the killings, atrocities and abuses of human rights in El Salvador and, like all Canadians, we deplore them. Bilaterally, we have made frequent representations to the government of El Salvador. Multilaterally, we have been among the most active of all states in fora such as the OAS and the United Nations in seeking to mobilize international opinion in favour of a greater respect for human rights in the Salvadorian conflict. During the current session of the UN Human Rights Commission we are actively working for a constructive resolution which will call for a restoration of respect for human rights and an end to all arms supplies to all parties in El Salvador.
As for the future, we believe that there is an urgent need for a political settlement which will enable the moderate democratic elements in the government of El Salvador and in the revolutionary forces to coalesce. Canada welcomes the first signs of a willingness to negotiate on the part of the government. The president of El Salvador, Mr. Duarte, has recently indicated that his government is prepared to have a dialogue with the revolutionary forces, and it is now up to those forces to respond. We have no illusions that the process will be easy, since the more extreme elements on both sides will resist making the concessions necessary for a lasting solution. In the interim, the revolutionary forces should cease undermining the efforts of the government to introduce its reform package, and both sides should take immediate steps to stamp out mindless violence.
Having made those points, it should be remembered that historically Canada has not had strong or important links with El Salvador. It is a country near our part of the world but hardly a neighbour. However, the human tragedy of El Salvador has engaged the attention of all countries.

March 9, 1981
El Salvador
In this situation, what are our responsibilities? The first is to try to inform ourselves so that when we discuss these issues we at least do so knowledgeably. Even this is not easy. Much of our information is indirect and partial. It is refracted through the prisms of particular points of view before it reaches us. Views conflict and there is even conflict about matters of fact.
In the circumstances, the views of countries near El Salvador or with more important interests in El Salvador than Canada are more important to us. We note that some of these countries, whose views we respect, have taken a stand close to our own. There has yet been no initiative to refer the situation in El Salvador to the United Nations, nor is it being dealt with in the OAS. I also believe that this motion is rather naive as it does not take into account the various implications and ramifications of the situation prevailing in that country, while on the other hand, the motion seems to me slightly pretentious as it purports to be based on a thorough knowledge of the factual reality in that unfortunate country.
Mr. Speaker, no one questions the fact that in Central America as in the Latin American continent as a whole, socioeconomic conditions are so horrendous that they literally make visitors to these countries sick to their stomachs. I had the opportunity to live for two years in South America and I can understand the feelings of exasperation and frustration of a working class exploited by oligarchies with the support of governments which to say the least tolerate those inequities. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, these problems must be solved by the people of those countries. In the case of El Salvador, the last thing to wish for would be a massive presence or intervention by any foreign interest.
Mr. Speaker, the motion gives the impression that we are living in a world where there are only good guys and bad guys, where everything is either black or white. In other words,
March 9, 1981

unfortunately, this motion does not consider all the hues of the complex situation now existing in El Salvador. For instance, this motion assumes naively, to say the least, that the United States, our southern neighbours, are the only country to provide military aid to one of the parties in the conflict. It also suggests, quite wrongly, that it was basically the United States of America which decided to become militarily involved in El Salvador. Absolutely nothing is said about interventions by other interests, countries or ideological groups. There is complete silence in that regard. What about Cuba? No, Cuba is completely out. Even though the Nicaraguan territory has been used, this is completely ignored in the motion.
Mr. Speaker, when the Canadian people have given a group of men the responsibility to govern their country, and when these men have decisions or judgments to make about situations outside our borders, I believe the least we can expect is that they should be quite familiar with the facts. I think that unfortunately, as far as the situation in El Salvador and the rest of Central America is concerned, we have to be extremely cautious, otherwise we might make judgments which will not serve the interests of Canada and the free world, or even of the people in countries like El Salvador who deserve a better fate.
I would like to close by quoting the words of the former American ambassador to El Salvador, Mr. Robert White, who has, on several occasions, publicly opposed the military aid given by his own country to the junta which governs El Salvador. Mr. White, who saw the situation first hand for a few years and who witnessed the events in that country, wrote the following-I say all this, Mr. Speaker, to show that everything is not either black or white and that it is not only a fight between the good guys and the bad guys-as I was saying, Mr. White stated the following, as reported by The New York Times on March 7, only two days ago, and I quote:

No leader of the leftist forces, whether it be Ungo or (Roman) Nayorga or (Hector) Oqueli, has ever-and I have asked that they do so publicly-made any effort to stop the leftist forces from murdering, kidnapping, assassinating. The left takes bus drivers out of their vehicles and guns them down in front of the people. The day that Dr. Ungo condemns that, he starts to gain some moral authority in my eyes. The government of Napoleon Duarte, on the other hand, and many of the moderate military officers, have explicitly condemned the excesses of the security forces. They have tried and thrown out a large number of enlisted people and have transferred a number of officers out of the line of command.

Mr. Speaker, 1 will conclude in pointing out that conditions are not as simple as we are led to believe, that the United States have to assume their responsibilities in the face of strategic interests and on behalf of world peace and also because we cannot allow the setting up of another Cuba on the doorstep of the United States we can deplore such conditions, but if we have to ask the American government to stop such arms shipments we should in the first place make sure that arms shipments from other sources do not reach El Salvador.

Mr. Speaker, I, too, am proud to join with my colleagues and participate in this historic debate. I am also pleased and proud to support the joint resolution which is before us, although I must admit that I feel somewhat intimidated because of the immensity and complexity of the legal, political and social questions with which we are dealing.
I have never been much of a constitutional buff, Mr. Speaker. Constitutions are such difficult, abstract things that I doubt if debating them will ever become a national pastime. Despite efforts of the official opposition and the provinces to hype this matter up, I get as many letters complaining about poor postal service as I do about the so-called constitutional controversy. That is not to say that constitutional questions are unimportant. They are incredibly important.
My constitutional experiences, first here in this House, later in Room 200 and now back again in this chamber, have taught
8180

March 12, 1981
The Constitution
me a number of valuable lessons, some of which I would like to talk about at this point. First, there exists a vast array of public groups who feel that their fundamental rights and freedoms have not always been protected by our present Constitution and that the Constitution needs to be amended in order to provide us with a charter of rights and freedoms. The groups ranged all the way from natives to Japanese Canadians, to the handicapped, women's groups and civil libertarians, to name only a few. Many of these people, and more, demand an entrenched charter, and they are opposed to waiting for one any longer. The hooker, though, is that a constitutional amendment is required to add such a charter to our Constitution. Unhappily, as everyone knows by now, the provinces will not agree on an amending formula and they have not been able to agree for over 50 years.
So here is our constitutional Catch-22-no provincial agreement, no amending formula; no amending formula, no charter; no charter, no unified protection of rights allowed to Canadians right across our nation.
For those who complain about the proposed amending formula giving regions unwarranted veto powers, what we now have, and have had, is a practice through federal-provincial conferences which permits every province, large or small, to have a veto-and that has been our problem. I believe those in the Conservative Party who counsel us to bring the BNA Act home as is and add a charter later with the help of the provinces are either mischievous, naive or stupid. The most effective way to deny Canadians a charter for another 50 years is to take that advice.
The second point which can perhaps be dealt with in fewer words but which is no less important, is that from some of the items we have read and heard, such as "Canadians should not be asking the British to amend our Constitution" and "Let us build our Constitution here", one would almost conclude that this whole debate is taking place thousands of miles away in far-off and mythical Albion. Before Christmas I asked myself, "Where am I?" I answered, "In Room 200." Then I asked myself, "Where is Room 200?" I answered, "On Parliament Hill." I said, "Well, where is Parliament Hill?" I answered, "In Canada." "What are we doing here?", I asked myself. I answered, "We are building a Constitution." Now again today I pinch myself and ask myself, "Where am I?"

While we all recognize that words are sometimes inadequate vehicles to convey ideas and that intensity of feeling rather than substance is the order of the day, I believe we have dwelt too much upon the process of constitutional reform and have not addressed ourselves enough to the content of constitutional reform.
I do not wish to dwell at length on the issue of the amending formula, save to say that without one which is fair and equitable, both rigid and flexible, and cognizant of our federal character, our definition of a truly federal state falls short of the mark. All constitutional authorities agree that the provincial legislatures have the right to amend their constitution as it affects them, save with regard to the offices of lieutenant governors. Yet Canada's national legislature cannot do so at its own discretion without the consent of the parliament of Great Britain. Thus, Canada is relegated to being the only free nation in the world which is not at liberty to change its Constitution without the consent of another sovereign state. For any province, court of appeal or person to suggest that this government's proposed Canada Act, Constitution Act and the patriation instruments are in themselves unconstitutional is inappropriate, in that such a view or judgment serves only to suborn the right of this central government to act.

No member of this House has higher authority than that which is transferred by the electorate.

If an amending formula is not achieved, the federal government reserves the exclusive right

Let me review briefly how this confederation all came about. The country of Canada is a federal state. It is a federation which is controlled and has been controlled since 1867 by the British North America Act. This act was designed for Canadians by Canadians. It outlined the responsibilities of the central government, as opposed to the responsibilities of the provincial governments. It fulfilled a necessity within our federated system. It dictated that divisions beyond reach or easy access to consensus of opinion would not alter the way the country was designed to be run.
There were some very good reasons why the British North America Act was designed in that fashion: So there would be control, and so that not one of the 11 involved governments would be able to act unilaterally to change the direction and the intent of the BN A Act. years. Discussions which took place in which Canada played a major role, this being the senior dominion, and the Statute of Westminster became a reality. It was written in that statute that the British parliament would henceforth have no further direct control over the "Dominions" included in that statute. Canada was a motivating force in the writing of the Statute of Westminster and, interestingly enough, Canada was to be the only exception.

The answer is, quite simply, we were concerned in that day and age, just as we should be today, that no single government would have the opportunity to override the jurisdiction of another. Much to the chagrin and the sorrow of Great Britain, we insisted that Canada be made an exception to the Statute of Westminster and that we continue with the jurisdiction given under the British North America Act. Mr. Speaker, I think it is apparent that there is a good deal of sentiment, both in Parliament and in society in general, in favour of doing a great deal more than we are to overcome problems facing disabled persons. This is not just a passing sentiment related to this year's observance of the International Year of the Disabled; our awareness of the handicaps which society creates for the disabled has been growing for some years.
The House can be especially grateful for the work of the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. Its hearings across the country and the report which it published on February 16 have done a great deal to increase public awareness and understanding of the needs of disabled persons and to suggest ways of improving their situation.
The question of paper currency and what might be done to help blind persons identify the various denominations is just one of the many issues which have been raised and must be faced. The bill before us proposes the use of Braille markings to differentiate between different values of bank notes. There are differing views as to whether Braille is the best identification method, but there will be general agreement that there is a problem for blind persons in dealing with our paper currency. Some blind people have adopted special ways of folding their paper money to permit quick identification when they pay bills. Whether or not they do this, they must still rely on sighted persons at some stage to sort out the currency for them.
I should like to say at the outset that this question has been and is under careful consideration by the Bank of Canada. Officials of the bank have been in consultation with the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and the Canadian Council of the Blind. They have also studied approaches to the problem which have been adopted in other countries.
The use of Braille on banknotes is not supported by either of the two organizations, the CNIB or the Canadian Council of the Blind, which is an association of blind persons. There are two main reasons given for this. First, the raised dots of Braille can become flattened and indistinct as a banknote becomes worn. Second, only a small portion of blind persons-perhaps 5 per cent or 6 per cent of the 33,500 blind persons who are registered with the CNIB-use Braille regularly.
There are, however, other approaches which can be considered. Those who are registered as blind have less than 10 per cent of their vision. But not all of these are totally blind; perhaps 80 per cent or more of them have what is termed "guiding vision". For example, many of them can read the numerals on bank notes if they are sufficiently large and in contrasting colours or shades of black and white.
Another approach which has been under consideration involves differing sizes of bank notes for the various denominations. This is the approach recommended a few years ago in a report called "Vision Canada", which was commissioned by the CNIB in co-operation with the Department of National
March 19, 1981

Health and Welfare. This is the approach which the CNIB has tended to favour.
The recent report by the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped urged that action be taken soon to make our currency more easily identifiable by blind or visionally impaired persons. Although that committee did not recommend any specific method, it did mention that other countries use different sizes of currency. There are quite a few countries outside North America which have currency of various sizes, depending on denomination. I suspect that this developed historically, for reasons other than to assist the blind. But it could be an obvious aid to a blind person provided there is a sufficient difference in size to make the different denominations readily distinguishable. That is the case in Britain, which has three main bank notes, the one, five and ten pound note, with marked differences in size. On the other hand, Canada has six main denominations ranging from one dollar to 50 dollars. I am not sure whether the six bank notes could be adequately differentiated in size without creating an oversize bill.
One other approach which has been adopted by a few countries is to use a system of tactile codes to identify the different bank notes. These involve raised dots, circles or other markings which are a good deal larger than the Braille dots. The codes are simple and easily learned. These codes are now in use on the bank notes of The Netherlands, Belgium, Switzerland and Israel, all countries which also have varying sizes of currency. Several other countries are considering adopting a similar approach.
I suggest that from the evidence available there are several approaches which should be considered in trying to meet the goal in this bill put forward by the hon. member for Portage-Marquette (Mr. Mayer). Since there are some concerns about the effectiveness of using Braille, as proposed in this bill, I suggest we should not give it second reading. However, I believe we should refer the subject matter to committee, and I understand the government is prepared to do just that.
I should also like to mention that the matter is under careful consideration by the Bank of Canada, and I feel confident that today's debate will help in reaching a decision on this very important question.

We have never done it. I say there it is, Madam Speaker, and that makes Citation 311 just as much a part of the rules of procedure of this House as are the citations regarding parliamentary language on which you have to rely, as are the citations regarding naming members, which has to be done once in awhile, as are the citations about privilege or points of order or the ringing of the bells. Indeed, though 1 have contended that we are governed by citations as much as we are by rules, I would point out that Standing Order 1 does say that:
In all cases not provided for hereafter or by sessional or other orders, the usages and customs of the House of Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland as in force at the time shall be followed so far as they may be applicable to this House.
1 say that in Britain, where they have had Hansard much longer than have we, there has never been a deviation from the rule that the only speeches printed in Hansard are those that were delivered. As a matter of fact, they do not even permit the appendices and things like that which we add at the back of our copies of Hansard. They are as strict as citation 311 says, that under no circumstances may speeches which have not been delivered be put into Hansard.
I contend that this is a violation of a tradition of 100 years in this House, and longer in Britain. I maintain that it is just as much a part of our rules as are the things that had to be contended with today: privilege, points of order, ringing of the bells and unparliamentary language. All of these things are governed by the citations and by the practices, and we should stay with them. The same is true about the printing of speeches.
1 think 1 have fairly well kept my promise not to get into the merits of the issue as to whether or not it is a good idea. 1 am sticking to this as a point of order. I believe Your Honour
should rule that paragraph (e) at the end of this motion, which would permit speeches to be handed in and printed in Hansard, is out of order. As I say, it is not an attempt to change the rules on a permanent basis. Neither is it something that has been put there as a sessional order because there has been consultation with the other parties-there has been no such consultation.
I note in respect of other things that are being set aside for the purposes of this motion that there is a reference to orders that need to be changed, there is the word "notwithstanding" and so on. We find references to Standing Order 6(1) and Standing Order 40; somewhere else there is the word "notwithstanding", and so forth. But when it comes to this departure from a century's practice, there is not even the word "notwithstanding". There is not any suggestion that this change in the rules is one to which the House should consent.
Therefore, I contend that we should not have to debate this when we get to the motion. This is why I sought to raise the point of order right away, even before Your Honour put the motion. 1 contend that Your Honour should rule paragraph (e) out of order and that it should be stricken from the motion now before the House.

I have a theory which I should like to develop in the 30 seconds or so left to me. We have available the best educated work force in the world because of accessibility of schools and educational programs. Because of medicare, we have the healthiest people in the world. We need portability because the average Canadian worker will change jobs no less than six times in his lifetime, and female workers more than six times. If the private pension industry cannot meet that challenge within a reasonable period of time, then the Canadian public will demand that the government take steps. I do not believe in more regulation; I believe in less, but most regulations I am aware of are forced on the government. and the employee, not only the federal and provincial governments, not only members from all parties in the House, but participation by the interested spokesmen on behalf of the industry. Just as we were forced into maternity benefits because private industry refused to meet that responsibility. The record shows that the national government has always been ready to ensure that oil sands and heavy oil projects will take place. Therefore, the National Energy Program has established a policy of steadily rising incentives to find this oil. It has been estimated that netbacks will almost quadruple during this decade. This will assure orderly development of this declining resource.

To get
back to the matter before you, Madam Speaker, the first question I raise for Your Honour to decide is: When the issue is the same and the court is the same, does the fact that the process is different make so overwhelming a difference that what would be illegal for us to do if this government had acted becomes legal for us to do because it was another government which got the same question to the same court? I remind Your Honour of your words on Friday when you said, and I quote:
Sub judice is a convention which is "a voluntary restraint imposed by the House upon itself in the interests of justice and fair play", as stated in Citation 335 of Beauchesne's fifth edition.
I think that is absolutely correct. The Chair will have to decide whether justice and fair play have to do with the substance of the question rather than with how many steps it took to raise the question or how many steps it took to get a contentious question before the court which must ultimately decide it.
I want to go back, if I might, to the principle of sub judice in our parliamentary system, and I would like to cite briefly from the nineteenth edition of Erskine May, page 427. The general principle is stated as follows:
Matters awaiting the adjudication of a court of law should not be brought forward in debate, subject to the right of the House to legislate on any matter-
In other words, that does not preclude the right of this Parliament to act on matters which might be before the courts in the application of existing law. But, when there are questions which relate to the substance of that law, the principle stated by Erskine May is quite clear:
Following the first report of the Select Committee on Procedure, 1962-63, the House passed a Resolution-
That was on July 23, 1963.
_-which set out the rule in detail. This resolution bars references in debate-
As well as in motions and questions.
-to matters awaiting or under adjudication in all courts exercising a criminal jurisdiction and in courts martial from the moment the law is set in motion by a charge being made to the time when verdict and sentence have been announced, and again-
This is germane.
-when notice of appeal is given until the appeal is decided-
There is then some reference to courts martial, which is not relevant here.
The resolution of 23 July 1963 also applies to the civil courts, and in general it bars reference to matters awaiting or under adjudication in a civil court from the time that the case has been set down for trial or otherwise brought before the court, as for example by notice of motion for an injunction; such matters may be referred to before such date unless it appears to the Chair that there is a real and substantial danger of prejudice to the trial of the case; the ban again applies when notice of appeal is given until judgment is given.
So the appeal procedure, which is the matter we are dealing with here, is very much within the practice cited by Erskine May.
On 28 June 1972 the House came to a further resolution, that notwithstanding the resolution of 23 July 1963 and subject to the discretion of the Chair, reference may be made in questions, motions or debate to matters awaiting or under adjudication in all civil courts, in so far as such matters relate to a ministerial decision which cannot be challenged in court except on grounds of misdirection or bad faith, or concern issues of national importance such as the national economy, public order or the essentials of life; and that in exercising its discretion the Chair should not allow reference to such matters if it appears that there is a real and substantial danger of prejudice to the proceedings-
Prejudice to the proceedings of the court is a matter to which I want to turn some attention now. I find it difficult to think of a prejudice to the proceedings of the court that is more dramatic or substantial than exporting the question to another country before our courts can decide on it. In my opinion, there is a very real and substantial danger, to quote the authorities, if the question that the Supreme Court wants to decide is rushed out of our country before the court has had a chance to consider it.

That seems to me to be a real and substantial danger of prejudice of the most extreme kind. I cannot think of prejudicing a court's decision in a more dramatic way than to, in effect, kidnap the question and get it out of the country before that court can become seized of it.
We are told part of the reason for this is that there is a timetable problem in Westminster; they want to deal with it more quickly. Well, I think we as Canadians, as a sovereign Parliament, have the right to ask why the timetable of Westminster should prevail over that of a Canadian court.

BasePK: 3291198

Speech:
Madam Speaker, I am very conscious of your ruling today on the point of order raised a few days ago by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). I want to impress upon Your Honour at the outset that my question of privilege raises a whole new point. It does not attempt to go over the ground which was so ably put forward by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition.
It is interesting that in Your Honour's ruling today, if I may refer to it-I am not questioning it; I accept it-you pointed out precedents of your illustrious predecessors in which they stated that the Chair was merely to rule on questions of order, not on questions of law; that it was not for the Chair to decide whether or not a question was constitutional, within the Constitution, or ultra vires of the Constitution; that, in fact, was a question for the courts to decide.
It is interesting that my question of privilege today arises out of just such a situation. It arises out of the unanimous ruling brought down earlier today by the appeal division of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland on questions submitted to it by the six provinces. It is not without interest that the ruling should come down on the thirty-second anniversary of the dominion of Newfoundland becoming the tenth province of Canada.
I intend to lay out what I consider to be a very important question of privilege arising out of the decision of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and the business before the House. The questions on which the court ruled were four in number, three of which were submitted by the six provinces; the fourth question dealing specifically with the terms of union between Newfoundland and Canada was submitted by the province of Newfoundland. It is important for me to read the questions because they are relevant. I think it is important that they should be on the record. Certainly in terms of my argument it is important that they be placed within the context of my question of privilege before Your Honour. They read as follows:

March 31, 1981
Privilege-Mr. McGrath
1.	If the amendments to the Constitution of Canada sought in the "Proposed Resolution for a Joint Address to Her Majesty the Queen respecting the Constitution of Canada", or any of them were enacted, would federal-provincial relationships or the powers, rights or privileges granted or secured by the Constitution of Canada to the provinces, their legislatures or governments be affected and, if so, in what respect or respects?
2.	Is it constitutional convention that the House of Commons and Senate of Canada will not request Her Majesty the Queen to lay before the Parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland a measure to amend the Constitution of Canada affecting federal-provincial relationships or the powers, rights or privileges granted or secured by the Constitutions of Canada to the provinces, their legislatures or governments without first obtaining the agreement of the provinces?
3.	Is the agreement of the provinces of Canada constitutionally required for amendment to the Constitution of Canada where such amendment affects federal-provincial relationships or alters the powers, rights or privileges granted or secured by the Constitution of Canada to the provinces, their legislatures or governments?
The fourth question was the one submitted by the government of Newfoundland; it deals specifically with the terms of union. It reads:
4.	If Part V of the proposed resolution referred to in question 1 is enacted and proclaimed into force could
(a)	the Terms of Union, including terms 2 and 17 thereof contained in the Schedule to the British North America Act, 1949 (12-13 George VI, c. 22 (U.K.)), or
(b)	section 3 of the British North America Act, 1871 (34-35 Victoria, c. 28 (U.K.))
be amended directly or indirectly pursuant to Part V without the consent of the government, legislature or a majority of the people of the province of Newfoundland voting in a referendum held pursuant to Part V?
On each question the Court of Appeal of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland unanimously ruled in favour of the provinces. I intend to place before Your Honour arguments indicating that this decision directly affects my privileges as a member of this House. Today I am speaking to a matter of personal privilege. I should like to refer to Beauchesne's fifth edition, Citation 16, which reads in part as follows:
The distinctive mark of a privilege is its ancillary character. The privileges of Parliament are rights which are "absolutely necessary for the due execution of its powers". They are enjoyed by individual members, because the House cannot perform its functions without unimpeded use of the services of its Members; and by each House for the protection of its members and the vindication of its own authority and dignity.
Also in that citation Beauchesne refers to Sir Erskine May's Treatise on the Law, Privileges, Proceedings and Usage of Parliament, nineteenth edition, 1976, at page 67.
It bears repetition to note what Beauchesne said, that the House cannot perform its function without the unimpeded use of the services of its members and by each House for the protection of its members and the vindication of its own authority and dignity. I am being asked, as a member of this House, to do something which the courts have ruled to be illegal. That speaks directly to what Beauchesne had to say. Obviously, it is something that I cannot do. I cannot stand in my place and vote on a resolution that has been declared to be ultra vires and, hence, illegal. To do so would be flying in the face of the trust I have of the people who elected me to represent them here. But, more particularly, I would be flying in the face of the solemn obligation that I have as a member of this House to uphold the rule of law.

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission, my comments will be about the use of Standing Order 75c and the need to reform the rules of the House rather than about the bill in respect of which the order is being used.
During the Thirtieth Parliament, the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization studied the question of reform of the rules of the House. Unfortunately, there was no action at the time in spite of much good will and hard work by members on all sides of the House. One particular proposition which received a good deal of attention at that time was the suggestion that, at the second reading stage, which is approval in principle, the debate be limited to one day and that the major debate on a bill should occur at third reading, after the committee has made whatever amendments seem appropriate following the hearing of witnesses. This is a proposal which I hope will be considered again and, perhaps, acted on shortly in this session.
What happens now at second reading stage is that we tend to have lengthy speeches. A long speech is not necessarily designed to be persuasive, to advance an argument or increase understanding. We have long speeches at second reading. We have the same points discussed in committee, again at report stage and again at third reading. I think members on all sides of the House suffer from this process because when fewer members can participate, both supporters of the government and members of the opposition feel frustrated. They do not feel the same sense of commitment toward dealing with the business of the House in an orderly fashion.
In the case of the bill before us, the borrowing authority, there were five days of debate at second reading before 75c was introduced, since it was not possible to reach an agreement to limit debate in any way. We then had another two days of debate after 75c was moved. This is a practice which seems to be taking place so often with our bills.
Recently I came across a definition of "nation" in St. Augustine's "the City of God" which read as follows:
A nation is an association of reasonable beings united in a peaceful sharing of the things they cherish.
I know many members of the opposition share that view. Very often when we work on committee, we are able to subordinate our partisan differences and work in a constructive fashion. We can expose our differences, but we do it with the intention of arriving at some common ground. Certainly as Canadians, when an all-party delegation goes abroad, usually we are able to agree among ourselves that we will present honestly our differences of opinion based on our different ideologies, but also, in the national interest, we try to present a reasonable picture of the things upon which we agree as Canadians.
What has been happening to the nation's business in recent days has been dispiriting. There has been a lot of name-calling which has been unsophisticated and unseemly. These have not been the highest days in the history of Parliament. While structural changes such as changes in the rules of the House will not solve all these problems, I think they would assist. With shorter speeches, with more work done in committee, with more opportunities for all of us to participate, we could reduce a lot of the unnecessary irritants in the House. We will always have differences of principle and differences of opinion, but it is urgent that we try to reduce some of the unnecessary irritants.
The eighteenth century definition that the role of opposition is "to oppose" is surely very old-fashioned for us. Surely, what is needed in our time is much more opportunity for members of the opposition and supporters of the government to work constructively together, recognizing some basic differences, and to be prepared occasionally to make more than a normal effort to find middle ground.
One of the big changes I should like to see, whenever we get around to discussing the rules of the House seriously, is a change in the rules of question period. In Westminster, sup-
April 2, 1981

porters of the government can ask questions, just as members of the opposition can. In this House there has been a tradition that question period is the prerogative of the opposition. I think three Speakers have held that supporters of the government are able to get information in other ways. This is true, but I think our constituents have a right to see us representing their interests publicly; they should not always have to depend on faith and assume that we are pursuing their interests in caucus. It should be possible for those who have elected supporters of the government to see us expressing our concern for the interests of our constituents in exactly the same manner as members of the opposition can.
So, these are some of the issues which I trust will be addressed soon in Parliament. I know all members of the House would like to see some changes in the rules of the House which would enable us all to do our jobs more effectively and hopefully would reduce the number of occasions when Standing Order 75c or similar motions would have to be called into play.

This would mean that the borrowing authority bill could not be brought in until probably December, or perhaps January. This makes a relatively tight legislative time frame within which to bring forward a borrowing authority bill, get it through second reading, into committee, back for report stage, third reading and royal assent after going through the Senate as well. We are talking about a very tight fiscal time-frame in which to get the borrowing authority bill through.
It makes sense to have a fall budgetary cycle for many reasons. One is that having your budgets in the late fall would allow the provinces to see what the federal fiscal framework will look like and, therefore, plan their budgets more effectively, and, typically, they come in the spring. In fact, we have had very good reaction from the provinces in respect of that kind of a suggestion at the December meeting of finance ministers. We were discussing when they would like to see a federal budget and the kind of consultation and interaction they would like between the two levels of government in order that budgetary cycles of all governments could be more closely integrated with better co-ordination than we have now. I think that is a good process.
In doing this, as I said, it does place the federal government in a rather peculiar situation, having a very short time-span from the point at which the budget is brought down to the fiscal year end when new borrowing authority has to be implemented. As a result, this non-lapsing component of the
current borrowing authority bill gives us flexibility if contingencies occur so the bill cannot be brought forward, as in the event of an election, for example, which was the case on February 18, 1980. Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss this important motion before the House under Standing Order 75c. This government is attempting to tell us that this is simply an allocation of time, that it is not closure motion and was never intended to be such. In actual fact, if one reads what the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Bussieres) said when he moved this motion, he will see the motion, as reported at page 8830 of Hansard for March 31 states the following:
-for the purpose of this order and, in turn, every question then necessary in order to dispose of the stage of the bill then under consideration shall be put forthwith and successively, without further debate or amendment.
The "Oxford Illustrated Dictionary" defines closure in Parliament as a decision by vote of the House of Commons to put a question without further debate.
Members of the government are attempting to tell us that this is simply an allocation of time. Like many other things that happen in the House, they say one thing and do another.
I should like to take you back to the 1969 debate when Mr. Blair, who was in charge of the committee which brought in 75c stated, as reported at page 10957 of Hansard for July 8:
I would like to say first of all with reference to Standing Order 75c that it cannot be invoked unilaterally by the government.
I should like to know how it is being invoked if it is not being invoked unilaterally. It is binding on our side and not binding on the government. Only the government can bring it
in.
Now, Mr. Speaker, they are telling us it is an allocation of time. But here we have a bill for $14 billion which the
April 2, 1981

government wishes to pass, and they want to allocate the minimum amount of time for debate. I would like to quote Mr. Blair, the chairman of that committee in 1969 when he said:
I think what I have said is clearly on record.
There will be at least ten days of time in this debate. Well, Mr. Speaker, there has not been ten days of time in this debate. He also said that there would be at least three days of debate in committee, and there were only two days of debate in committee. We can go on and on, but this is not allocation of time, it is just another method of closure.
What do they really want to do? They want to borrow $14 billion when we know that as of March 26 they had $6.4 billion. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) admitted that they still had $4.8 billion, which means they spent $1.6 billion in one week. The Minister of Finance admitted in committee that the government needs approximately $1 billion a month more than they receive. Why do they need to borrow $14 billion when they have $4.8 billion left? And at the rate at which they admitted they were spending more than they were taking in, they only need $1 billion. So it is quite obvious that this government does not know what they are spending.
I would like to quote the Minister of Finance further. He said five months ago that inflation was going to be 10 per cent, and admitted last week that it was 12.2 per cent. When did he have that revelation? Obviously he did not know five months ago, yet the deputy governor of the Bank of Canada admitted in committee that they are able to define inflation six months ahead. How come the Bank of Canada knew we were going to have 12 per cent inflation but the Minister of Finance did not? He still does not know. He does not know what inflation is going to be next month.
This government does not need the $14 billion it wishes to borrow; it is a sham. If it needed the money, we would be more than happy to pass it the bill, but it is quite obvious that the minister admitted they did not yet need to borrow the money. But, he says, one of these days they will.
In conclusion, there is no need to impose Standing Order 75c. This government brought it in in 1969 to limit debate and it is just another way that this government is going to close off debate, and that is why over the last week we have been attempting to bring this government to order so that they will be responsible for what they are doing.

It only borrows funds to spend. What are we doing for industrial development in this country? What has the government done in 13 years? Nothing. Does the government realize that at current rates of interest, without any additional borrowing, if it stopped today and said that it would not borrow any more money, our debt would amount to $200 billion by 1986? That would be the result if we voted in this House not to permit any further borrowing; our debt would still be $200 billion. That is assuming there were no additional deficits and that the government did not require any money. That is assuming the interest rate, which is now in place because of this inflationary spiral, continues.
Furthermore, does the government realize that by 1986-is less than five years away-the interest to carry this debt will amount to $1,000 for each man, woman and child in this country? Let us assume that an average Canadian family consists of 3.5 people, a mother and father and 1.5 children. Assuming that, the amount of $3,500 has to be brought home by the wage earner just for the government to pay the bill. I plead with the government to stop coming back to the trough. We are destroying ourselves and our country. We must stop doing that and we
must stop now. We have run out of goodwill overseas. Where do we go next to borrow money if we are turned down?
The government keeps borrowing additional sums to buy up private corporations. Do hon. members realize that every time a private corporation is purchased a taxpayer is eliminated? Once a company becomes a Crown corporation, it does not earn any money. That is why we are borrowing more money- to buy corporations that can become non-profit organizations. Such a procedure erodes our tax base. It erodes the chance for this country to have a balanced budget.
I maintain it is time for the government to stop borrowing money and start to encourage the private sector instead. expert study and for recommendation to the House, and to the policy committee which would study the bills with a view to making amendments.

good many programs which developed after that, including the Agricultural and Rural Development Act, commonly known as ARDA, the Fund for Rural Economic Development, which was known as FRED, the Atlantic Development Board was created, the Area Development Incentives Act was brought before the House and, finally DREE was created.

My responsibility with the Progressive Conservative Party is in respect of the young wing of the party and of youth concerns. I feel it is incumbent upon me to address this House on this legislation, a bill which has some very long term ramifications for our justice system.
Let me start by saying we agree with the concept of greater rights, greater responsibilities and greater flexibility in dealing with the rehabilitation of young offenders. This is a very good concept. It is long overdue. I am not even going to touch on the subject of its history as that has been covered by my colleagues.
I should like to touch upon a few subjects, the first being age. Under Clause 2(1) of Bill C-61, a child is defined as being anyone who is or appears to be under the age of 12 years; it defines a young person as anyone who is or appears to be over the age of 12 and under the age of 18.
There is also a provision in the same clause that the governor-in-council may issue a proclamation at the request of a province to establish the maximum age of a young person as being either under the age of 17 or 16 years.
The consequence of this provision is that the youth court would have exclusive jurisdiction in respect of an offence committed by a young person between the ages of 12 and 16, or 17 or 18. A person under the age of 12 is to be subject to provincial child welfare legislation. Where the individual is over the age of 16, 17 or 18, he would be subject to ordinary criminal law and the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts.
The change effected by Bill C-61 is that the minimum age of jurisdiction of the youth court is to be increased from 7 to 12 years, and the maximum age is to be increased from 16 to 18 years with the possibility of a reduction rather than an increase, as is presently the case under the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
The effect of increasing the minimum age is that the youth population which will be subject to provincial laws and social welfare programs alone will increase dramatically. This will put a tremendous additional cost on the provinces. Of course, we are interested to find out if there is any increased funding in view of the shuffling off of these responsibilities to the social welfare programs of the provinces. It also would have the effect of decriminalizing any delinquent acts committed by those who are under the minimum age. The effect of raising the maximum age would be to increase the number of young people who would be subject to the juvenile justice system at the upper age limit and require that a province request explicitly that this be reduced. Despite many attempts over the years to establish a uniform maximum age across the country, the
April 15, 1981

federal and provincial governments have been unable to come to an agreement on this issue, and I think that is unfortunate.
The inequity in our justice system across the country has been well covered today. People will be treated differently because of their ages. Let us look at what would be the effect if we were to have agreement on an amending formula. Let us therefore examine the amending formula which the opposition now favours. After proposing three amending formulas,

April 22, 1981
The Constitution
including one which would have required unanimity and one proposed after the committee hearings which would have provided for opting out of a charter of rights, the Tories have come with their fifth preferred formula.
First, the amendment contains a provision whereby constitutional amendments may be enacted following the approval of seven legislatures representing 50 per cent of the population. After it has been approved, amendments would normally be made by seven provinces with 50 per cent of the population. In other words, as a general rule, constitutional amendments could be made without the consent of all the provinces. For example, amendment would be possible with British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan opposed. Or, to take another example, Quebec, or Quebec and New Brunswick, would no longer be ensured of a voice in the protection of the French language at the federal level.

We know what that means. It means that with that formula, a majority in Parliament plus seven provinces could decide that in the future French would no longer be spoken in the House; that we would be denied the use of the official language of our choice in federal courts; that in all federal institutions in which we are represented we would no longer have any bilingualism; that the Official Languages Act soon to be enshrined in our Constitution, to protect it against the whims of the majorities, could be abrogated precisely on the whim of the majorities, without the Quebecers or even one or two of the other provinces favourably disposed toward the French fact being able to do anything about it. That is why, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative proposal is totally unacceptable to us.
Second, while the amending formula would be adopted by seven legislatures representing 50 per cent of the population, it would be only natural that it be changed in the same way. However, that is not the case. For some reason, changes to the amending formula will require unanimity. Here all provinces will acquire a veto right. The logic is less than overwhelming.
The Tory party will drop the referendum provision for breaking deadlocks. Despite a history of being unable to agree on constitutional change in Canada, the opposition does not see the need for a deadlock-breaking mechanism. Despite our democratic traditions, they do not trust the people to break deadlocks between governments.
What is the effect of not having a deadlock-breaking mechanism? Let me give an example. The federal Conservative party is in favour of a charter of rights as being the will of Canadians. They have said that many times. However, they propose an amending formula whereby a charter of rights can only come into effect if approved by seven provinces. In other words, it could be vetoed by any four Premiers.
The Tory proposal will not allow this veto to be tested in a referendum whereby Canadians could express their will. I will
give an example. The six biggest provinces in Canada represent 88 per cent of the Canadian population, roughly 22 million people. The four smaller provinces represent about 12 per cent of the population, roughly three million people. The motion before the House calls for a new budget, and we agree. The other day and also in the past our financial critic, on behalf of our party, outlined a number of measures which would be appropriate in a new budget, not simply to deal with the question of inflation, but to deal with the long-range structural problem of the Canadian economy which must be dealt with if we are to have full employment.
Today I want to deal with those measures, specifically in the context of dealing with the question of inflation in a serious way. I hope the government will have the honesty today to do what it did not do yesterday in the debate: that is, to reply to the points which are made; not to sit there in arrogant indifference while listening to what is being said on this side of the House, but to take on the arguments. If our arguments are shown to be wrong, we will admit they are wrong. However, we want this serious matter dealt with in a serious way.
Before going to three of four very specific suggestions on how to deal with inflation, I must say that although I have indicated my party agrees with some of the suggestions which the official opposition has made in terms of dealing with inflation, there is one matter on which we frankly cannot accept any criticism from their corner, and that is the interest rate policy itself.
The Leader of the Opposition should know better than anyone else in the House of Commons, perhaps, in spite of his own criticism as Leader of the Opposition before he became prime minister, that when he was in office interest rates not only went up one, two or three times, but more than that. So when it comes to interest rate policy, neither we nor anyone else has to listen to the Conservative Party of Canada. However, I want to put that aside. The Liberal party is the government of the day and it has the responsibility to deal with the important matter before us.
I now want to suggest three or four specific ways of dealing particularly with the pervasive problem of inflation. In so doing, I repeat that I want to see the government put up or shut up today and to respond to the arguments. More than respond to the arguments, I would like to see the government act on them if it agrees with them.
First is the question of interest rates. I have already said that the evidence is overwhelmingly clear to everyone, except someone who gets so rigidly locked into some economic theory that he decides to lock out all the evidence, that the increase in interest rates has not resulted at all in a reduction of the cost of living but has had the opposite effect.
What do we say should be done? We are saying that instead of sitting back and responding in a knee-jerk reaction to what takes place in the United States in terms of interest rates, we should move in the opposite direction. At his regular meetings with the Governor of the Bank of Canada, or by telephone, the Minister of Finance should make it clear that he expects the Bank of Canada to start moving immediately, step by step, in the direction of a reduced interest rate policy in order to bring
The Economy
interest rates down to roughly the level of inflation in Canada. We think that would work.
I want to say to the Minister of Finance that if there is a run on the dollar or if there is a concern about a flow of money south of the border in the short run, then certain action could be taken. We do not withdraw from the suggestion of a form of exchange controls. The minister should know better than anyone else that some form of exchange controls has been put in place by many countries in western Europe and by the United States. In fact, the administration of John F. Kennedy in 1963 and that of Richard Nixon in the early 1970s introduced special measures to deal with the problem of the outflow of capital. They showed a little more imagination than has been demonstrated by the Government of Canada. When President Kennedy was in office he introduced for a limited period of time a special tax intended to discourage the outflow of capital. That practice was duplicated almost a decade later by President Nixon.
I say to the Minister of Finance that it is hardly a radical idea and hardly a profound change. Some countries in Europe and also the United States have done this. I repeat, this party does not back away from a little innovation. If we need a limited form of control to deal with a possible export of capital, then the New Democratic Party says, "Let's do it if it benefits the people of Canada".

From our perspective, this policy on land claims is somewhat anachronistic in light of the recent constitutional steps taken by Parliament as a whole.
After eight years, the 1973 land claims policy is a document which is outmoded in the context of the recent constitutional recognition of aboriginal rights.
The 1973 policy required the extinguishment of "native interest" in certain lands in exchange for some kind of compensation. It further limited negotiations only to areas where native title had never been extinguished by treaty or superseded by law.
The policy's provisions had the effect of smoothing the way for resource developers in the north by extinguishing aboriginal title, and in the south by precluding negotiations in areas where resource developers were already established.

The prime rate is 18 per cent, as opposed to 19.06 per cent in Canada. That is as of May 5. I suppose the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance must be living in the same kind of airy-fairy world as his mentor, the Minister of Finance, and must not really be aware of the true situation.
It is tragic in the extreme, Mr. Speaker, that for over a year the Minister of Finance has been in his portfolio and has yet to come up with anything vaguely resembling an economic policy. In fact, the only policy he has now is to let the Bank of Canada pursue its tight money policy. The Bank of Canada has for several years been operating on the theory that if you control the money supply, keep it within certain limits, this will eventually bring down the rate of inflation to that level. Well, that policy has been in place for several years now and during that time inflation rates have in fact climbed, and we now have enough experience to make the empirical judgment that that is a bad policy.
However, Mr. Speaker, one does not need just to make that empirical observation; in fact, examining the policy for what it is raises all kinds of questions about its validity. For example, there is the mere question of the kind of money, if you will, that the Bank of Canada is controlling. Their policy is to control the so called Ml, which is currency and demand deposits, within a limit of 5 to 9 per cent and they have now
May 21, 1981

dropped that down to 4 to 8 per cent. In fact, Mr. Speaker, there was a raging argument several years ago, and it continues in this country, the United States and Europe, as to whether Ml represents an adequate definition of money, and many suggest that M3 should be used, which is currency and all chequable notices and term deposits plus foreign currencies. If we look at M3 over the last few years, we see it has been growing at a rate more closely analogous to the inflation rate. It has been growing at 12, 14, 16 per cent, while Ml has been growing at between 5 and 9 per cent. So perhaps those who argue that the Bank of Canada is controlling the wrong type of money have a pretty valid argument based on the performance that we have observed so far.
Moreover, Ml merely represents transactional money. The theory is that if you control and limit that, you limit the transactional ability of the economy to progress by limiting the ability of people to spend and invest, thereby taking some of the steam out of the economy and producing a lower inflation rate. Well, one of the experts in regard to interest rates, I suppose on a global basis but certainly in the United States, is Henry Kaufman, chief economist with Salomon Brothers, a very well known and highly reputed Wall Street firm. He has consistently and very accurately predicted high interest rates over the last decade and dismissed the impact of money supply on interest rates. He points out in an article in Fortune magazine of May, 1981:
"One of the great wonders of the world", he says, "is the American credit market." In his view, bankers over the last two decades have been dismayingly creative in attracting new types of deposits and finetuning "spreads" between their cost of money and their selling price, so that they can turn a profit no matter how much they pay for deposits.
The net result is that there is no discount rate that the Central Bank imposes which will affect the profits of banks. In fact, as the leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broad-bent) points out, profits tend to go up under those circumstances. He then goes on to say that what really matters in terms of money and inflation in the economy is the credit involved; not the currency or the transactional money, but use of credit. He gives examples of the kind of creativity shown by modern bankers and financial officers with corporations. I quote:
"The financial markets are very innovative, and we're going to find some more substitutes for money," says Kaufman. "We can drive that credit mechanism very hard." Thus he forsees an increase in the velocity of money far beyond past experience.
The net effect of that, as he says here, is that not only have high interest rates not dampened the creation of credit and therefore the flow of money, but it has merely added to the cost.

BasePK: 3299886

Speech:
Madam Speaker, it is the sad task of Parliament today to pay tribute to the memory of one of its most distinguished former members. The passing of David Lewis has deprived Canada of a man of passionate commitment, a man of ideas and conscience, a brilliant and eloquent person, a man who devoted the whole of his adult life to the service of others.
Canada's loss is felt nowhere more keenly than here in Parliament, a place he loved and honoured. It was here, as Leader of the New Democratic Party, that he found the fullest scope for the expression of his ideals and idealism. It was here that he was able to speak to Canadians, day in and day out, about social and economic justice, about the gap between what Canada was and could become, about the primary duty of Parliament to help and protect those who could not protect themselves.
By giving expression to his own profound belief that political action is the noblest and most effective means of achieving social change, he also lent added dignity and respect to the profession of politics, and to the Canadian political process.
Because he became best known to Canadians during his tenure as Leader of the New Democratic Party, it is sometimes forgotten that he was a political activist in the cause of social democracy for some forty-four years of his life.
His was a life-long commitment, played out principally away from the limelight of the national leadership, in the hard-slogging and frugal years organizing, travelling, and speaking in every part of Canada.
It was that commitment which gave power and forcefulness to his public performance. He was not one to play at politics for a time while waiting for more lucrative doors to open. He gave his life to politics, as his chosen way of giving his life to his country and its people.
David Lewis was a man in whom social idealism was combined with the most practical of political skills. He excelled as a strategist and orator, as a campaigner and organizer.
He knew every detail of the cost of every victory he won, because he had paid that cost in his own hard work.
He was a proud Canadian, imbued with the sense of wonder of one who was not born in this country. He both shamed and inspired many native-born Canadians by learning not just one of our official languages, but both of them, and he spoke them fluently. That was also a sign of his commitment to Canada and to all its people.
As we mourn the passing of this dedicated human being, our sympathy goes out to his beloved wife, Sophie, and to his family. May the knowledge of the great respect he earned throughout a life of service to Canada comfort them in this time of bereavement.
