BasePK: 3300586

Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) sought an explanation of the taxes on alcoholic beverages in his questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on May 15, 1981.
The Excise Act and the Excise Tax Act impose commodity taxes on most goods imported into or manufactured in Canada. The great majority of these taxes are ad valorem levies; that is to say, they are expressed as a percentage on the sale price. The federal sales tax which is the main levy, is imposed at the rate of 9 per cent on most goods, except building materials, which are subject to a 5 per cent rate.
Since the federal sales tax is a percentage of the price, it automatically increases as prices increase. No special mechanism is required to achieve that relationship. Indeed, the system has functioned in that manner for more than 75 years.

May 26, 1981
Adjournment Debate
However, in the case of alcoholic beverages and tobacco products the commodity tax levies are structured somewhat differently. The bulk of the taxes on these goods are not expressed as a percentage of the price. Rather, they are expressed as an amount per unit of product. To illustrate, the levy on spirits was $16.25 per proof gallon of alcohol, and the levy on beer was 42 cents per gallon. These specific levies were increased in April, 1980 to $17.15 per gallon for spirits and to 54 cents per gallon for beer.
In the absence of discreet changes in such specific levies on alcoholic beverages, their real value falls as prices rise. Even with the increase in April, 1980, the real value of taxes on these goods is less than it was in the late 1960s.
Federal revenues should keep up with the growth in prices of products, as do those provincial mark-ups which are expressed
in percentage terms, and as does the general sales tax which is imposed on most goods as a percentage of value.
For these reasons, the government introduced a measure to adjust automatically the levies on alcoholic beverages in line with changes in prices. While this change does increase federal taxes on these products, it does not discriminate against beer, wines and spirits. Rather, it places the commodity tax levies on those goods on approximately the same basis as the commodity tax levies on all other goods.

June 1, 1981

way of making an increase in the old age pension on an emergency basis.

Mr. Speaker, it is with interest that I rise to participate in the debate tonight on the opposition motion that deals with a condemnation of the government for "unnecessarily raising petroleum taxes and thereby burdening all consumers, but particularly consumers of heating oil, with prices far in excess of those promised without providing relief to those hardest hit and least able to cope."
June 8, 1981

This motion, put forward by the Conservative opposition, effectively says two things, Mr. Speaker. It is a condemnation not only of the government's policy with regard to energy, but a condemnation of the government for not protecting those who are supposedly, and in fact are, being hit by the rising price of oil and, by implication, high interest rates, and other things as well.
I should like to try to deal with those issues-the condemnation, the reasonableness of the condemnation of oil prices, the condemnation implied now, as it has been many times in the past in this House, of the other parts of the government's economic policy and the condemnation of the government for not assisting those who are being hard hit by rising prices across the board, and by high interest rates.
In the budget of October 28, the government promised essentially three things, Mr. Speaker. First, it promised to restrain spending and bring it within the trend line of the growth of the gross national product over a period of four years. Second, it promised to reorder government spending priorities toward a greater emphasis on economic development, industrial adjustment and manpower retraining. These programs have been introduced in order to try to help the people make the adjustments that all hon. members agree will be necessary in our daily working lives over the next several years. Finally, the government promised to follow a monetary policy consistent with the fight against inflation.
Let me deal first with the argument pertaining to oil prices. Today we heard members of the opposition claim that they would not have increased the price of oil nearly as fast as this government has done. This is a surprising statement because, basically, it just is not true.
In the past, as I probably will in the future, I have relied on the words of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) when he was minister of finance. I think he understood the realities of economic policy that face any minister of Finance, this country and the government. In his sombre moods, he is not swept away with the kind of rhetoric that some of the members of the opposition-and I hasten to point to the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald)-are swept away. The hon. member for St. John's West can be very rational. I have listened to what the hon. member has to say. I believe he follows me in this debate, at which time he will have something to say in response.
The hon. member for St. John's West appeared on the program "Question Period" yesterday. He was asked some penetrating questions and gave some honest and straightforward answers. I would like to relate some of the hon. member's responses that are very pertinent to today's debate. It says something about what the Conservative policy is, or what a responsible segment of that party believes the Conservative policy should be, and what their assessment of this government's policy is. In many cases, it is a very realistic and fair assessment.
Energy
The hon. member for St. John's West was asked what would happen to oil price increases and what the situation would have been under a Conservative government. He replied as follows:
Had we been there, we wouldn't be spending $5 billion on the oil imports subsidy. The price to the primary producer of a barrel of oil would have been higher and the oil imports subsidy considerably lower and the deficit considerably lower and then even with a mortgage interest and an energy tax credit we wouldn't have the deficit that we have today.
The implication, if I read that properly, is that if the oil import compensation payments are less, then oil prices have to be higher because the oil imports compensation payment is based on the differential between the domestic price and the foreign price. If the compensation payments are less, that means that either the world price is lower, which is not conceivable because it is outside of our control, or the domestic price would have to be higher, which is very conceivable. Not only that, but the price to the primary producer of a barrel of oil would have been much higher than under this government.
These are quotes from statements by the hon. member in "Question Period". He was asked how fast energy prices should rise in this country and whether it is necessary for energy prices to rise in this country. I think all members agree that it is necessary. The question was asked:
-how quickly do you think that we should move the price of domestic oil close to the world level? How fast should we move?
The hon. member replied:
Well, I think that we should-at least as fast as we were proposing a couple of years ago, certainly to 75 per cent over the next several years ... I don't think we should delay too long. We're babying ourselves too long now-
The hon. member was then asked:
Do you think we should move as fast as, say, three years to get our own oil prices on to a realistic, lasting level or should we spread it out over five, six, seven years.
The hon. member replied:
I think that three or four years should be plenty.

A variety of speakers in this debate have clearly articulated their concerns about indexation. We also heard from spokespersons in the financial community who condemned this approach and we heard from taxation people within and beyond government who questioned this approach as being logical or realistic.
Who are the financial advisers, the tax experts, the economists who claim that this is the correct approach for the government to use in collecting additional revenue? On whose behalf do they speak when suggesting the concept of indexing as set out in this bill? The concept of indexing is insidious in that it puts Canadian consumers at the mercy of foreign exchange differences. As inflation increases in a particular country and the value of that currency relative to ours changes, that fact may have a significant effect on the consumer price subgroup on which this particular index will be based.
If the cost of hops was to increase significantly in one year because of crop failures or the introduction of new equipment or machinery to the industry, for example-and I identify hops as one of the components of the particular consumer index subgroup-that would mean that the price of wines would also increase, the price of tobacco would increase and the price of distilled spirits would increase in this country. Is this what we want to see? Yet it is the situation which hon. members opposite consider to be logical.
When all of us are concerned, to quote the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), with "wrestling inflation to the ground", it is important that we realize that indexation is a confirmation of the mind set that inflation is with us for some time to come.

Mr. Speaker, I want to indicate that we will support the amendment with respect to fishing and fishing equipment. I want to remind the House that the government's amendment is based on the illusion that one can readily distinguish between equipment which is used for commercial fishing and equipment which is used for sports fishing. The amendment replaces an existing section which is different and enumerates all the items to be exempt from the sales tax, as follows:
Fishing nets and nettings of all kinds; specially designed needles for use in repairing Fishing nets; metal panel devices for use in keeping nets open; metal swivels; fish hooks, lures, jiggers and artificial baits; sinkers and floats including trawl kegs;
The section goes on to say:
-none of the foregoing for sports fishing purposes:
This is based on the illusion that one can readily distinguish between equipment which is sold for the purpose of fishing for sport and equipment used for commercial fishing. Who makes the distinction? Is it the store owner who decides that someone is going to be engaged in sports fishing, or is it the manufacturer who decides what equipment is going to be used in one domain and not the other?
I find it a little strange that the government would exempt an objective number of items that are described in such detail. It describes the interstices of each piece of twine and says which will be exempt.
At the end of this objective definition it introduces an entirely subjective notion, which is the purpose for which the article is intended. That is the kind of thing that can lead to invidious distinction and petty hardship for many inshore and offshore fishermen. I think it would be easier if this particular clause was dropped and the previous legislation retained.
As I am from a land-locked constituency-the old constituency of Broadview once opened on to Lake Ontario so I was not land-locked all the time, but Broadview-Greenwood has been cut off from the sea so I do not get extensive correspondence from fishermen-I would appreciate it if the minister would tell us how many complaints have been received from the industry and from the fishermen involved about the previous section and why it is necessary to replace it with this one.
I suspect that the accountants in the Department of Finance decided that they had discovered some discrepancy between this and the perfectly rational system they are looking for with such almost absurd persistence, and they are responsible for this amendment rather than having concern for the needs of the people in the industry.

The alcohol and tobacco tax has always been a flat tax, in dollar terms. In other words, the tax was explained in the following way: the federal government tax or the provincial government tax, because both place taxes on certain products, will be 35 cents per pack of cigarettes. That is an example. That being the case, it was a very unusual tax. A fixed dollar levy is a tax which does not apply in many other areas in our society. Most taxes are on a percentage basis. The sales tax in Ontario is 7 per cent. The manufacturers' excise tax, which was formerly 12 per cent, is now 9 per cent.
There are other forms of taxes. The income tax provides that if one makes a certain amount of money, a certain percentage of that will come to the federal government and a certain percentage will go to the provincial government. The taxes are stated on a percentage basis. These two taxes, alcohol and tobacco, are stated on a dollar basis. As a result, as the price of the product goes up, the tax stays precisely the same. Speech:
Mr. Speaker, the matter I wish to raise this evening relates back to February and March of 1981. It concerns the decision of the Dart shipping group to move its container service from the Port of Halifax to the Port of Montreal in connection with a proposed liaison between the Dart shipping group and Canadian Pacific Limited.
In specific terms, on March 4, 1981, I questioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) with respect to the involvement of the Canadian National Railway Company in the operations of the Cast shipping group, which I considered, and which many in the Port of Halifax considered, to be interinvolved with the decision of the Dart shipping group to remove its operation to the Port of Montreal.
Mr. Speaker, one of the problems which has occurred in the last few years in relation to the North Atlantic container traffic is the competition which has driven many of the marine transportation companies out of business. It is apparent that there has been a consolidation of the marine transport service amongst a few international operators. One of these international operators is the organization which is apparently headed

Adjournment Debate
by a Canadian citizen who lives abroad, and who operates the Cast shipping group.
The decision of the Canadian National Railway Company, endorsed by the Government of Canada, to invest over $60 million in the Cast shipping group, has given the impression to the international marine transport companies that the Cast shipping group has the backing of the Canadian government. It was only reasonable then that the Dart shipping group, as well as other international marine transport companies, would seek to protect themselves from this kind of special deal which was provided by the Government of Canada through its agency, the Canadian National Railway Company.
Therefore, with that motivation in mind, the province of Nova Scotia, and other persons who were interested in the port of Halifax, sought the assistance of the Minister of Transport in reviewing the decision which was made by the Dart group and the Canadian Pacific Railway whereby the container service was removed, as I have said, from the port of Halifax to the port of Montreal. In specific terms, what the premier of the province of Nova Scotia asked the Minister of Transport to do was to hold an inquiry at which all of the factors which were relevant to this kind of decision-making would be reviewed.
The Minister of Transport indicated in this House of Commons and elsewhere that the whole matter could be reviewed by the Canadian Transport Commission at a hearing which was required under the National Transportation Act, because Canadian Pacific Limited, being a transport company, sought to acquire an interest in Dart.
That hearing was held last week in the city of Halifax; but unfortunately, at the very outset of the hearing it was stated in categorical terms by the representative of the Canadian Pacific Limited, that nothing will stop Dart's move to the port of Montreal. Consequently, Nova Scotians, from the premier of Nova Scotia right across to those interested in the port of Halifax and all citizens, were very disappointed because there was no way that this whole decision could be reviewed.
We have repercussions because in the U.S. Congress and before a committee of the United States Congress objections have been raised to the operation of the Cast shipping group. It has been described as a James Bond company, robbing traffic from U.S. marine carriers and taking them to Canadian ports. On the face of it, there might seem to be some advantages for Canada; but after all, we are a very small country dealing with the United States goliath.
I can guarantee Your Honour and all hon. members of this House that if the United States retaliates against these predatory moves by the Cast shipping group, which are said to have the support of the Government of Canada, and are said in that congressional hearing to be a flag carrier of Canada, it will be a disaster for the Canadian marine industry. It will be a disaster because the United States has that kind of power, so much so that our Canadian embassy had to send a diplomatic note asking that a bill proposed by the Congress of the United States to enact these measures which would protect the U.S. marine industry be delayed and not passed by the Congress.
This is the kind of problem that arises from the government's involvement. Encouraging Dart to move from the port of Halifax to the port of Montreal not only affects the port of Halifax, it has international repercussions as well. If allegations have been made, they must be answered by the Minister of Transport. The only way they can be properly answered is at a full hearing. We can review the whole marine transportation industry in relation to container traffic and get the answers-not only the answers necessary to protect the port of Halifax from the predatory moves of the port of Montreal, but also the answers that will stave off the criticism now being vented in the United States and which could have very serious repercussions.
The Minister of Transport has a serious obligation in this area. I can understand how he would seek to protect the port of Montreal by writing off $230 million in debts and by providing millions of dollars worth of infrastructure for that port, but by doing so he is going to create an international controversy and wreak havoc in the marine industry in Canada.

This bill is intended to give further impetus to the energy conservation activities of the government. It also draws attention to that part of the National Energy Program which I regret has not received as much attention as the supply side; that is the need to conserve energy in Canada. We have had in place for some time a program intended to reduce the consumption of all forms of energy in the industrial sector. Earlier today the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources made reference to the co-operative arrangements that have been worked out between industry and government to give substance to our commitment to reduce the use of energy in the manufacturing industry in particular.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that Canada is one of the world's heaviest users of energy, but that of course is understandable given our vast territory, small population and an often hostile climate. Nevertheless, those factors should not be seen as an excuse for extravagance in our use of energy. Therefore, the conservation efforts embodied in the NEP, indeed in this bill, take on a special importance.
In addition to the industrial initiatives I mentioned, the NEP also envisages new rules regarding residential units which will be implemented as of tomorrow. Hon. members may have seen in the newspapers in the last few days the requirement that no new residential unit will receive federal assistance or guarantees if it is heated by oil, unless no other reasonable energy alternative exists.
In addition to the building requirements, we have embarked upon a program four years ago to promote better insulation in residences. CHIP is familiar to hon. members of the House; I need not dwell on it. It is the principal method of providing funds to encourage greater energy efficiency in our homes. Currently the residential sector accounts for approximately 15 per cent of primary oil use in Canada. We believe that through CHIP which was initiated in 1977 the federal government will be able to encourage a reduction in the consumption of oil and thereby contribute to our total goal of self-sufficiency by the end of this decade.
We have set some substantial targets for a reduction in home heating oil consumption. Home owners are clearly responding to the incentives we are providing through CHIP grants. In 1977 only 15,000 grants were made, whereas the estimate for 1980-81 is for a total of 500,000. This is clearly a
Canadian Home Insulation Program
substantial increase. Our present goal is to reduce by one-third the oil used for space heating in reinsulating residences.
The bill before us this evening draws attention to the benefits of the insulation program. It will also bring to mind, in the case of some hon. members and in the case of the public, the need to ensure that high standards are maintained in the insulation industry. The government has moved to ensure that certification becomes a basic feature of the total program. We have worked with the Canadian General Standards Board to develop a certification program for home insulation which will be in place on November 1 of this year. Indeed, after that date it will be mandatory for all contractors performing work under CHIP to be certified if they wish to continue in the industry. Equally, we have embarked upon a major program review to determine the extent to which CHIP has met its initial targets and to explore any modifications which may be needed in light of experience.
In our view, the program has proven to be a major success. It is an important feature of the total National Energy Program and indeed of the energy future of Canada. In terms of reducing Canada's demand for imported oil, the program has already reduced our needs by something over $2 billion.
I could continue with some more details about the program, but I hope my necessarily brief introduction is sufficient for a bill which I trust will win the immediate support of all hon. members of the House.

As everyone knows, the western economy depends heavily on the export of raw materials. If the transportation system does not have the capacity to move them, the economy of the west, indeed of the country, will suffer.
Some months ago, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said in the House that he was not willing to consider changes to the Crow rate unless there was a consensus in the west that changes had to be made. In my view, Mr. Speaker, more and more westerners are now realizing that this is not just an agricultural issue but one that affects western economic development in general, and they are speaking out. As a responsible westerner, I am sure the hon. member does his best each weekend to build the consensus that the government is seeking. I hope he encourages his colleagues to do the same.
